title: Remove Wallpaper Without Damaging Drywall
description: Torn drywall paper is the costly wallpaper-removal mistake. Step-by-step: test, score, soak, peel, clean off adhesive, and repair before painting.
h1: How to Remove Wallpaper Without Wrecking the Drywall
heroIntro: Most wallpaper comes off cleanly with patience and the right solution. Rushing it, or pulling paper that was hung on unprimed drywall, is what tears the wall and turns a weekend job into a repair project.
excerpt: Torn drywall paper is the costly wallpaper-removal mistake. How to test, score, soak, peel, and clean off adhesive before you paint.

sections.h2: Why wallpaper damages some walls and not others
body: Drywall is a gypsum core wrapped in a paper face. If the drywall was primed or sealed before the wallpaper went up, the adhesive bonded to that sealed surface and will release when softened. If the installer hung wallpaper directly on bare drywall, which was common in builder-grade homes, the paste soaked into the paper face itself. Pull the wallpaper and you pull the face of the drywall with it, exposing the brown kraft paper underneath.

Age and layering make it harder. Many older North Central Florida homes have two or three layers of paper, sometimes with paint rolled over the top, and each layer slows the stripper from reaching the original paste. Heat and humidity over the years can also bake adhesive into the wall. None of this makes the job impossible; it simply means more soaking time and smaller sections.
You cannot fully know which you have until you start, but a careful test in an inconspicuous spot, such as behind a door or where a piece of furniture will sit, tells you how cautious you need to be.

sections.h2: Identify the type of wallpaper first
body: Wallpaper comes in a few basic constructions, and each one comes off differently:
bullets: Strippable: the whole sheet peels off dry, often leaving very little behind. Lift a corner with a putty knife and pull slowly at a low angle.
Peelable: the vinyl top layer peels off dry but leaves a paper backing on the wall that has to be soaked and scraped.
Traditional paper or grasscloth: absorbs water readily and usually comes off with soaking.
Vinyl-coated or painted-over paper: water cannot penetrate, so the surface must be scored or the top layer removed first.

body: Prepare the room before touching the walls. Turn off power to the room at the breaker, remove outlet covers and switch plates, and cover the outlets with tape. Lay plastic and absorbent drop cloths along the baseboards, since this is a wet job.
bullets: Peel off any layer that comes away dry. Removing the vinyl face lets the solution reach the paste.
If the surface resists water, score it lightly with a scoring tool. Use gentle pressure; pressing hard punctures the drywall face.
Mix a wallpaper stripper solution. An enzyme-based stripper works well, and many people have success with hot water and a little fabric softener or dish soap.
Apply the solution generously with a pump sprayer or sponge to one section at a time, and let it soak for 10 to 15 minutes, keeping it wet.
Scrape gently with a wide, flexible plastic or rounded-corner scraper, working with the paper rather than digging into the wall. If it fights you, apply more solution and wait longer.
For stubborn sections, a wallpaper steamer can help, but keep it moving so you do not soak and soften the drywall face.

body: The step people skip is washing off the leftover paste. Old wallpaper adhesive is water-soluble and stays that way. Paint applied over it can crack, crackle, or peel, and the moisture in latex paint can reactivate the adhesive under the new coat.

Wash the walls with warm water and a little stripper or a dedicated adhesive remover, rinse with clean water, and let them dry completely. Rub your hand across the wall when it is dry: if it feels slick or sticky, wash again. Once the wall is truly clean, it is ready for repairs.
Even with care, small areas of drywall face may tear. Do not apply joint compound directly over torn, fuzzy brown paper. Water in the compound will make the paper bubble.
bullets: Cut away loose paper with a sharp utility knife and lightly sand any fuzz.
Seal the exposed area with an oil-based or shellac-based primer designed for damaged drywall paper, or a specialty sealer made for this purpose.
Once dry, skim the area with joint compound, feathering beyond the damage, and sand smooth. Larger damaged walls may need a full skim coat.
Prime the entire wall with a drywall primer before painting so the patched and original areas absorb paint evenly.

sections.h2: Florida considerations: humidity and hidden mildew
body: In humid homes, especially bathrooms, wallpaper can hide mildew or moisture damage on the drywall behind it. If you find black spotting, soft board, or a musty odor once the paper is off, treat the mildew and find the moisture source before finishing. Bathrooms that lack an exhaust fan should get one, or the problem will return under paint as well. Badly damaged board should be cut out and replaced; our drywall repair and patching service handles that before painting.

Running the air conditioning or a dehumidifier while the walls dry speeds up the process and helps avoid soaking the drywall for long periods. Give the walls at least a full day to dry after the final rinse before you skim or prime, and longer in a closed bathroom.

sections.h2: When to bring in a professional
body: Strippable paper in a small room is a manageable DIY project. Multiple layers, paper painted over, paper hung on unprimed drywall, and large rooms or tall stairwells are where professional help saves time and the walls. Homes built before 1978 may have lead paint on top of or under old wallpaper, so test before sanding.

faqs.q: What is the easiest way to remove wallpaper?
faqs.a: Start by peeling any layer that comes off dry. Then soak the remaining paper with a stripper solution or hot water and let it work for 10 to 15 minutes before scraping gently. Patience is more effective than force.

faqs.q: How do I fix drywall after wallpaper tore the paper face?
faqs.a: Cut away loose paper, seal the exposed brown paper with an oil-based or shellac-based primer or a specialty sealer, then skim with joint compound, sand, and prime the whole wall before painting.

faqs.q: Can I paint over wallpaper glue?
faqs.a: No. Leftover adhesive can cause the new paint to crack or peel. Wash the walls until they no longer feel slick or sticky, let them dry, and prime before painting.

faqs.q: Can I paint over wallpaper instead of removing it?
faqs.a: It is possible on well-bonded paper with the right primer, but seams often show and the paper can loosen. Removing it and preparing the drywall gives a more reliable finish.
